researchers.name: Manu Kapur
researchers.known_for: Coined and developed Productive Failure — problem-solving before instruction improves conceptual understanding and transfer; 2021 meta-analysis with Sinha and 2024 trade book 'Productive Failure'

researchers.name: Paul Kirschner
researchers.known_for: Lead author of Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) 'Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work' — the canonical case for explicit, fully guided instruction for novices

researchers.name: John Sweller
researchers.known_for: Cognitive Load Theory and the worked-example effect; argues novices learn best from studying worked solutions, not from unguided search

researchers.name: Richard E. Clark
researchers.known_for: Co-author of the 2006 minimal-guidance critique; long-standing skeptic of discovery, inquiry, and constructivist teaching methods

researchers.name: Robert Bjork
researchers.known_for: Desirable difficulties — conditions that slow initial performance (retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving) but improve long-term retention; theoretical warrant for making learners struggle

researchers.name: Michelene (Micki) Chi
researchers.known_for: ICAP framework (Interactive > Constructive > Active > Passive); evidence that generative/interactive engagement beats passive receipt — supports questioning over telling

researchers.name: Kurt VanLehn
researchers.known_for: 2011 meta-analysis showing human tutoring yields d≈0.79 (not Bloom's 2 sigma) and step-based intelligent tutoring systems are nearly as effective (d≈0.76); deflated the human-tutor mystique

researchers.name: Kenneth Koedinger
researchers.known_for: Cognitive Tutors and the 'assistance dilemma' (with Aleven, 2007): when does giving information help vs. withholding it — frames answer-withholding as an optimization problem, not a doctrine

researchers.name: Dorottya Demszky
researchers.known_for: NLP for education; 'conversational uptake' measures of how tutors build on student talk; empirical grounding for what good tutor moves look like in dialogue data

researchers.name: Rose E. Wang
researchers.known_for: Bridge and Tutor CoPilot — showing LLMs underperform expert human tutors on remediation decisions, and that expert-thought-annotated data can close part of the gap
researchers.camp: Education NLP / skeptical of vanilla LLM tutoring

researchers.name: Arnav Gudibande & Eric Wallace
researchers.known_for: 'The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs' (2023): small models fine-tuned on teacher outputs copy style and fool crowdworkers but close little of the actual capability gap

researchers.name: Chunting Zhou et al.
researchers.known_for: LIMA (2023) and the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis: knowledge lives in pretraining; alignment/fine-tuning mostly teaches format and style — 1,000 curated examples can suffice
researchers.camp: Distillation optimists (style is cheap to instill)

researchers.name: Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, Jeff Dean
researchers.known_for: 'Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network' (2015) — the founding paper of knowledge distillation via soft teacher targets

researchers.name: LearnLM team
researchers.known_for: Pedagogy-informed fine-tuning of Gemini; evidence that tutoring behavior (including not blurting answers) can be trained into weights and preferred by expert raters over GPT-4o

frameworks.name: Productive Failure
frameworks.description: Sequence problem-solving BEFORE instruction: students generate (mostly failed) solution attempts, which activate prior knowledge and prepare them to learn from subsequent consolidation. Requires careful task design plus teacher-led consolidation — the failure phase alone is not enough.
frameworks.citation: Kapur, M. (2008) Cognition and Instruction; Sinha, T. & Kapur, M. (2021) Review of Educational Research, 91(5)

frameworks.name: Cognitive Load Theory / worked-example effect
frameworks.description: Working memory is severely limited for novel information; unguided problem search wastes capacity on means-ends analysis instead of schema building. Novices learn more from worked examples; guidance can fade as expertise grows (expertise reversal effect, Kalyuga).
frameworks.citation: Sweller, J. (1988) Cognitive Science; Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Educational Psychologist, 41(2)

frameworks.name: Desirable Difficulties
frameworks.description: Manipulations that impair short-term performance (retrieval practice, spacing, generation) enhance long-term retention and transfer — but only when the learner can eventually succeed; difficulties become undesirable when the learner lacks the background to overcome them.
frameworks.citation: Bjork, R.A. (1994) in Metacognition: Knowing About Knowing; Bjork & Bjork (2011)

frameworks.name: ICAP framework
frameworks.description: Learning outcomes ordered Interactive > Constructive > Active > Passive. Socratic dialogue sits in the Interactive/Constructive band — its advantage comes from forcing generation, not from answer secrecy per se.
frameworks.citation: Chi, M.T.H. & Wylie, R. (2014) Educational Psychologist, 49(4)

frameworks.name: Assistance Dilemma
frameworks.description: Frames tutoring as balancing giving vs. withholding information: both over-assistance (shallow learning) and under-assistance (floundering, frustration) hurt. Optimal assistance depends on learner prior knowledge, task stage, and error type — a direct challenge to blanket 'never give the answer' rules.
frameworks.citation: Koedinger, K.R. & Aleven, V. (2007) Educational Psychology Review, 19

frameworks.name: Scaffolding / contingent tutoring
frameworks.description: Effective tutors are contingent: they escalate help only after failure and fade it after success (Wood's 'contingent shift' rule). Socratic questioning is one rung on a help ladder, not the whole ladder.
frameworks.citation: Wood, D., Bruner, J. & Ross, G. (1976) Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2)

frameworks.name: Knowledge Distillation
frameworks.description: Train a small student on a large teacher's output distribution (soft targets) or generated data (sequence-level KD). Modern behavior distillation fine-tunes small open models on teacher-generated dialogues to transfer interaction patterns.
frameworks.citation: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015) arXiv:1503.02531; Kim & Rush (2016) sequence-level KD

frameworks.name: Superficial Alignment Hypothesis
frameworks.description: A model's knowledge and capabilities come almost entirely from pretraining; alignment fine-tuning teaches which subdistribution of formats/styles to use. Corollary: a small, highly curated SFT set can instill a stable interaction style — good news for teaching a persistent Socratic persona to an SLM.
frameworks.citation: Zhou, C. et al. (2023) 'LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment' arXiv:2305.11206

frameworks.name: Shallow safety/constraint alignment
frameworks.description: Fine-tuned behavioral constraints often live in the first few output tokens and collapse under prefill, paraphrase, or multi-turn pressure; making constraints 'more than a few tokens deep' requires training on trajectories where the model recovers mid-response.
frameworks.citation: Qi, X. et al. (2024) 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' arXiv:2406.05946

frameworks.name: LoRA vs full fine-tuning trade-off
frameworks.description: LoRA learns less new behavior than full fine-tuning but also forgets less of the base model's capabilities — directly relevant to instilling a tutoring persona without catastrophic forgetting of subject knowledge in a small model.
frameworks.citation: Biderman, D. et al. (2024) 'LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less' arXiv:2405.09673

debates.topic: Should learning start with instruction or with struggle?
debates.conventional: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006): novices should be explicitly shown what to do; minimal-guidance methods fail because they overload working memory and let errors compound.
debates.challenger: Problem-solving-first (with subsequent instruction) beats instruction-first on conceptual understanding and transfer when tasks and consolidation are well designed; the 2021 meta-analysis found reliable positive effects, larger for older students and high-fidelity implementations.

debates.topic: Is human tutoring really a 2-sigma intervention?
debates.conventional: Bloom (1984): one-on-one tutoring produces 2-standard-deviation gains — the benchmark every AI tutor cites.
debates.challenger: VanLehn (2011) meta-analysis: human tutoring is actually d≈0.79, and step-based ITS reach d≈0.76 — near parity. The 2-sigma figure came from combining tutoring with mastery learning under unusual conditions.

debates.conventional: Socratic purism (embodied in Khanmigo's design): the tutor should question at nearly every turn and never reveal answers, forcing generation.
debates.challenger: The assistance dilemma and contingent-scaffolding research: blanket withholding under-assists; effective tutors give bottom-out help after repeated failure. Recent LLM-tutor studies find Socratic guidance raises later learning gains but learners rate it less efficient and may defect to answer-giving tools — frustration and dropout are real costs.
debates.challenger_name: Koedinger & Aleven; recent Socratic-LLM evaluation work (e.g. 'Discerning minds or generic tutors?', arXiv 2508.06583)

debates.topic: Can small models be made into real tutors by imitating a big teacher?
debates.conventional: Fine-tune an open SLM on GPT-4-generated tutoring dialogues and you get a cheap Khanmigo (the Alpaca/Vicuna-era assumption).
debates.challenger: Gudibande et al. (2023): imitation transfers style and instruction-following surface form, not capability — crowdworkers are fooled, targeted evals are not. But the flip side (LIMA, LearnLM) is that a tutoring PERSONA is mostly style, which is exactly what distillation transfers well — so a Socratic SLM is feasible precisely because the constraint is behavioral, while its subject-matter ceiling stays that of the base model.
debates.challenger_name: Gudibande & Wallace vs. Zhou et al. (LIMA) / Google LearnLM team

debates.topic: Do behavioral constraints trained into weights actually hold?
debates.conventional: SFT on consistent demonstrations makes the behavior reliable; a strong system prompt plus fine-tuning suffices.
debates.challenger: Constraint adherence is often shallow — concentrated in early tokens and brittle under multi-turn pressure, user insistence, or distribution shift; small models are worse at maintaining persona under adversarial prodding, so training data must include pressure-and-recovery examples, not just clean demonstrations.

findings.claim: Problem-solving before instruction (productive failure) outperforms instruction-then-practice on conceptual knowledge and transfer across 53+ studies; effects strengthen with higher grade levels and design fidelity to PF principles.
findings.source: Sinha & Kapur (2021), 'When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works', Review of Educational Research, 91(5)
findings.effect_size: overall g ≈ 0.36 favoring PF; substantially larger (≈0.8+) in high-fidelity implementations

findings.claim: Human tutoring effect is d≈0.79 (not 2.0), and step-based intelligent tutoring systems achieve d≈0.76 — software tutors that scaffold at the step level nearly match humans.
findings.source: VanLehn (2011), 'The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems', Educational Psychologist, 46(4)

findings.claim: Imitation models fine-tuned on ChatGPT outputs mimic style well enough to fool crowdworkers but close 'little to none' of the base-model-to-teacher gap on targeted capability evaluations; gains require better base models, not more imitation data.
findings.source: Gudibande et al. (2023), 'The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs', arXiv:2305.15717
findings.effect_size: crowdworker preference ≈ parity with ChatGPT; targeted evals ≈ 0% gap closure on weakly-covered tasks

findings.claim: 1,000 carefully curated SFT examples suffice to align a 65B model to a consistent assistant style, supporting the claim that interaction format is learned cheaply while knowledge comes from pretraining.
findings.source: Zhou et al. (2023), 'LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment', arXiv:2305.11206
findings.effect_size: LIMA responses equivalent or preferred vs GPT-4 in 43% of human comparisons

findings.claim: Pedagogy-informed fine-tuning measurably shifts tutor behavior: expert raters preferred LearnLM over GPT-4o for tutoring interactions by a wide margin, showing 'do not just give the answer' behavior can be trained into weights at scale.
findings.source: Google DeepMind LearnLM technical report, 'LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning' (2024)
findings.effect_size: experts preferred LearnLM over GPT-4o by ~31 percentage points

findings.claim: Students tutored by a Socratic-constrained LLM achieved higher learning gains in later sessions and adopted more understanding-driven strategies than students with an unconstrained LLM — but perceived the Socratic tutor as less efficient.
findings.source: Socratic-LLM guidance studies surfaced in 2025-26 evaluation literature (e.g. 'Discerning minds or generic tutors?', arXiv:2508.06583; CEUR Vol-3953 hybrid evaluation of Socratic dialogue)

findings.claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs substantially underperform expert human tutors on dialogic moves — deciding when to probe vs. tell, and remediating the actual student error rather than a generic one.
findings.source: Wang et al., 'Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making' (NAACL 2024); automating-pedagogical-evaluation line of work (OpenReview D1IaG1InPy)

findings.claim: LoRA fine-tuning forgets less of base-model capabilities than full fine-tuning at the cost of learning less target-domain behavior — a favorable trade for style-only behavior transfer into small models.
findings.source: Biderman et al. (2024), 'LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less', arXiv:2405.09673
findings.effect_size: TMLR 2024; consistent learning-vs-forgetting Pareto gap across code and math domains

findings.claim: Safety/behavior constraints instilled by fine-tuning are concentrated in the first few output tokens and collapse under prefill or persistent multi-turn attack; deepening alignment across the whole response distribution measurably hardens constraints.
findings.source: Qi et al. (2024), 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep', arXiv:2406.05946

adjacent_domains.insight: Decades of evidence that asking evocative questions outperforms telling for behavior change — but MI codifies WHEN to shift from asking to informing (elicit-provide-elicit), a ready-made template for a tutor's escalation policy instead of blanket answer-withholding.

Clinical teaching scripts force the learner to commit to a diagnosis BEFORE the preceptor teaches — commit-then-instruct mirrors productive failure and shows structured question protocols can be trained into time-pressed non-expert tutors, analogous to fine-tuning a small model on a fixed dialogue protocol.

Explaining a problem aloud to a non-answering listener resolves many bugs — evidence that the generation/self-explanation effect does the work, not the listener's intelligence; a small model that reliably prompts self-explanation can deliver value beyond its raw capability.

Jailbreak and persona-drift research is the closest empirical literature on 'will my model hold its constraint under user pressure' — red-teaming with escalating please-just-tell-me pressure and training on recovery trajectories transfers directly to testing an answer-withholding tutor.

Well-designed games teach mechanics through structured challenge without tutorials (e.g., Nintendo's level-design pedagogy): difficulty is sequenced so failure is informative and quick to retry — a design vocabulary for making a tutor's withheld answer feel like a solvable puzzle rather than stonewalling.

misconceptions.belief: The Socratic method means never revealing the answer.
misconceptions.reality: Expert tutors are contingent: they withhold while progress is possible and give bottom-out hints after repeated failure (assistance dilemma, contingent scaffolding). Historical Socratic dialogues themselves mix questions with substantial telling.

misconceptions.belief: One-on-one tutoring gives 2-sigma gains, so an AI tutor should target d = 2.0.
misconceptions.reality: VanLehn (2011): the replicated human-tutoring effect is d ≈ 0.79; Bloom's 2 sigma bundled tutoring with mastery learning and corrective feedback loops. Realistic AI-tutor targets are ~0.7-0.8.

misconceptions.belief: Struggle is always good for learning (misreading of desirable difficulties and productive failure).
misconceptions.reality: Difficulties are desirable only when the learner has the prerequisites to eventually succeed and the struggle phase is followed by consolidation/instruction; unguided floundering without follow-up instruction is unproductive failure.

misconceptions.belief: Fine-tuning a small model on GPT-4 tutoring transcripts makes it tutor as well as GPT-4.
misconceptions.reality: Imitation transfers surface style and dialogue moves, not subject-matter capability or error diagnosis (Gudibande et al. 2023). The Socratic persona is learnable; the model's math is still the base model's math — so scope the domain to what the base model already knows.

misconceptions.belief: A strong system prompt is enough to enforce answer-withholding; fine-tuning is overkill.
misconceptions.reality: Small models drift from prompted personas under multi-turn pressure and user insistence; weights-level tuning holds constraints far better, but even fine-tuned constraints are shallow unless training data includes user-pressure and mid-response-recovery examples (Qi et al. 2024).

misconceptions.belief: More fine-tuning data always yields better constraint adherence.
misconceptions.reality: Narrow, repetitive SFT data causes catastrophic forgetting of base capabilities and mode collapse into templated responses; LIMA-style small curated sets and LoRA-style low-intrusion tuning often preserve more of the knowledge the tutor needs.

misconceptions.belief: If students prefer the tutor and rate it helpful, it is teaching well.
misconceptions.reality: Learner preference and learning gains dissociate: answer-giving tutors are rated more efficient and pleasant while producing shallower gains; crowdworker preference similarly overrates imitation models. Evaluate with delayed post-tests and targeted probes, not satisfaction ratings.
